en: Wren! There you are. Come round where I can see you. My ears are gone, child, but my eyes still work.
Last night the bell on the point went quiet. Folk in grey robes rowed off with it, singing.
I felt it through the floorboards.
The Drowned Choir, they call themselves.
Seven bells keep the Old One sleeping, and they mean to take every one.
You have the ear I lost. You'll hear where the bells are hidden. The first one sang out from the east.
Past the tidepools, into the Brinewood. There's an old ship rotting in the mangroves. Start there.
Keep your lamp lit, keeper. I'll keep mine.
East, past the tidepools, to the Rotting Hull. Go on now. The light will be here when you're back.
The Tide Hook! A barbed iron hook on a long chain, still cold from the sea.
Press U to throw it. It bites into iron rings and carries you across, and it drags crates and small creatures back to you.
Wren rings the Tidebell. The note rolls down through the wreck and out across the bay.
Far under the water, something vast breathes out, and sleeps a little deeper.

Press the new key or button. %s cancels.
A barbed hook on a long line. Pulls small things in and Wren across gaps.
Heavy enough to crack boulders and flip armoured shells.
Moths that glow in the dark. Raise it to show what hides from light.
Catch the wind and glide from high places.
Looses arrows of frost that freeze water solid. It never runs out.
Swim deep water, and dive under it for a few breaths.
Its note shatters bone and shows the unseen.
Blow it outdoors and Mantle the sky-ray carries you to a woken Tidestone.
Dried puffers stuffed with blast-salt. Light, throw, step back.
A keeper's practice blade. Light and quick.
Forged in Cinderreach and quenched in the sea. Hits harder.
At full breath it sends a wave along its swing.
Stops small shots from the front while you walk.
Keeps the spray off. No protection to speak of.
Woven from shed scales. Hits hurt less.
Cut from the deep. Hits hurt far less.
Holds a potion or a sea sprite.
Holds a potion or a sea sprite.
Drink to refill every breath bubble.
If your last bubble pops, it breathes you back to life.
Each bell holds one phrase of the lullaby that keeps the Old One asleep.
Each one gives Wren another breath bubble.
The Saltmarrow light, small enough to carry. Keep it lit.
Shell coins. Saltmarrow's traders take them.
Smooth, frosted glass, worn round by the sea.
Points to the chests still shut.
Opens the way to this place's heart.
Opens one locked door in this place.
A Tidestone sleeps here. Touch it to wake it.
Tidestone. Mantle can't reach you in here.
Woken Tidestone. Find the Wayshell to fly between them.
Woken Tidestone. Mantle can fly you here.

Wren lifts the lamp and flashes it once: I'll go.
Dunstan shoulders a coil of rope and wanders off towards the smokehouse, very slowly.
Saltmarrow. Mind the lamp, mind the tide.
Barnacle Wall. Built to keep the sea out. The sea moved in anyway.
Brinewood. The roots drink the tide and give back only shade.
Mill Row. The sails turn whichever way the Old One breathes.
Edgewatch Bluff. North of here, the charts give up.
Brine Spring. Salt water, welling up a long way from the sea.
Ashfall Gate. The hills are warm here, like something asleep.
Bleached Strand. Whatever these bones were, the sea wore them white.
Vertebra Road. Follow the spine. It goes all the way down.
You've been inside that old hull. I can smell the bilge on you from here.
Keep going down, child. Bells like the dark, and the Choir likes it better.
Morning, keeper. Sea's gone flat as a plate. No birds, no fish. Not a ripple.
Hessa's been up by the lighthouse since dawn, waving that lamp at nothing. Go and see her.
So the bell's gone. I felt the quiet in my nets before anyone said a word.
If you're heading east, mind the tidepools. The scuttlers there have got bold.
Mind the tidepools, keeper. Bold little things, those scuttlers.
The hull in the mangroves? My grandad swore she was a bell ship once.
Carried the bells out to their towers, he said. Then the sea took her crew and left the ship.
Wren! Wren! Old Hessa's been shouting for you all morning!
Well. Shouting. You know how she shouts. She's up by the lighthouse.
Are you going on an adventure? A real one? Past the tidepools?
Bring me something good. A heron feather. Or a crab with three claws.
You went in the Rotting Hull?! Was it full of ghosts?
Mum says it's full of ghosts. I said I'd go and check. She said no.
Keeper. Good. Do me a kindness?
My smokehouse rack's come down, and Dunstan's got the only good rope in Saltmarrow.
Dunstan's down by the barrels, most likely. Asleep on his feet.
He said yes? Without grumbling? Keeper, you've a gift.
Come by when you're back. There'll be smoked eel, and you'll be eating it.
Smoked eel when you're back. That's a promise.
Bell's quiet. Sea's quiet. Even the gulls are quiet. Whole coast's holding its breath.
Marga sent you? Was she asking nicely?
...Hm. Tell her she'll have it by supper.
The Stonebreaker Mallet! An iron-bound head on an ash handle, heavy enough to dent an anvil.
Press its item key (U or I) to bring it down in front of you. It bursts cracked boulders, drives pegs into the floor and flips armoured shells.
Wren rings the Ember Bell. A low, warm note fills the foundry, and the furnaces settle.
Somewhere under the bay, the great breathing slows. The fire is banked and low.
For a thousand years, seven bells have kept the Old One asleep beneath the bay.
At every turn of the tide a keeper rang them. Lately, only one keeper was left.
Last night, out on the point at Saltmarrow, the oldest bell went quiet.
You found it. I felt the Point Bell ring through the floorboards, clear as morning.
One bell home. Six more out there, and the Choir after every one of them.
Take the keepers' old Wayshell. Blow it under open sky and it'll carry you to a woken Tidestone.
Wren got the Wayshell. Outdoors, open the map and pick a woken Tidestone to travel there.
The next bell is crying out from the Kiln, in Cinderreach. Go on. I'll keep the lamp lit.
Cinderreach, child. Follow the smoke to the Kiln. The lamp stays lit.
You got the bell back?! Can I hold it? Just for a second?
...Fine. But I'm telling everyone I nearly did.
The Glowmoth Lantern! Pale moths stir inside the glass, and the dark around you thins.
Press its item key (U or I) to raise it, and again to lower it. Things that hide from the light can't hide from it.
Wren rings the Moth Bell. A soft, clear note, and every lamp in the mire flickers at once.
The wisps settle like snow. Far away, something huge turns over in its sleep, and lies still.
The Kite Cloak! Old sailcloth stitched over a frame of cane, with a red kite painted on its back.
Press its item key (U or I) to throw it open and glide. A fan's wind will carry you further. Press the key again to come down.
Wren rings the Storm Bell. Its note goes out over the crags, and the wind drops to a breath.
Clouds part over the bay. Deep below, the great sleeper stirs.
The Frostfang Bow! Pale ash wood, tipped with two fangs of ice that never melt.
Press its item key (U or I) to loose an arrow of frost. It freezes water solid where it lands, and never runs out.
Wren rings the Frost Bell. Its note rings clear under the ice, and the old glacier settles.
Out in the bay, the frost on the water melts. Down in the deep, the sleeper stops shivering.
The Drowned Belfry: the Great Bell
The Diver's Helm! Old brass, a round glass window, and a smell of the sea that never quite leaves it.
Now you can swim deep water. Press its item key (U or I) while swimming to dive under for a few breaths, and attack to slash underwater.
Wren rings the Drowned Bell. Its note sinks through the green water, deeper than a bell should.
Far below, something vast turns in its sleep and settles. The tide along the Verge runs gentle.
Saltgrave Brink. Nothing that set out across this water ever came back.

A crab with three claws, sidling about in the pools. Wren scoops it up.
Three claws! THREE! Wren, you're the best keeper there's ever been.
Here. I found it in the shallows. Mum says pearls like this hold a breath of the sea.
I named him Admiral. He pinches.
There's the keeper. Sit. Eat. No, the whole thing.
And take this jar. Every keeper needs one, for whatever the sea sends.
Rack's holding. Dunstan even helped tie it, if you can believe it.
The bell! Good. But from the gallery I saw something huge thrashing on the Wreck Strand.
Choir nets, I'd wager. On the strand, just this side of the Hull. Go and see, then come back to me.
Are you going up to see Hessa? Can I come? ...She'll say no. She always says no.
One day I'll have a lamp like yours. A real one, not paper.
Will you teach me the signals? I know some. One flash is yes. Two is no.
And the long one is... I always forget the long one.
Wren holds up the lamp in a long, steady glow.
I'm here! The long one means I'm here. I won't forget again.
Yes, no, I'm here. Yes, no, I'm here. I'm practising.
I saw you coming home with the bell! I flashed my lantern at you. Did you see?
Hessa gave you the old keepers' shell? Then you're a proper keeper now.
When you're old, I'll take over. That's the plan.
Felt that through the boards. It's dreaming, Wren. Of every one of them you sang quiet.
Go and keep it company a while. Mantle knows the way down.
Still dreaming down there. I feel every breath of it in the boards.
First night in the old cave. Vael says cold keeps a keeper honest. I say it numbs my fingers.
Signals again. One flash, yes. Two, no. A long glow: I'm here. Hessa makes it look like breathing.
We practise with cloths over our eyes now, lamps in our laps. Vael is better at it than he lets on.
Something under the ice tonight. Not wind. A long, low sound, like crying, a long way down.
Vael lies with his ear to the ice for hours. I told him it's the glacier settling. He didn't laugh.
It's every night now. It isn't angry, Hessa. It's grieving. And every time we ring, it hurts.
I want to stop ringing the bells. I want to go down to it and sing instead.
Under it, in a later and shakier hand:
I told him keepers don't get to choose. I was wrong. If you ever read this, Vael, I'm sorry.
Pike's the name, Marlo Pike. If it's worth having in Saltmarrow, it crosses this counter first.
Glints only, mind. Shells and promises I can pick up off the beach for nothing.
Back again, young keeper? Go on, have a look.
You cracked that old hull open! The puffers are back in the shallows, fat as you like.
Dried, and stuffed with blast-salt. Keep them well away from that lamp of yours.
Pleasure doing business. Mind how you go.
Quiet tides now. Good for trade. Good for sleeping, too, I find.
A keeper's cap. Haven't seen one of those up the pass in years.
That's the Kiln. Every bell on this coast was poured in there. Bronze, and the Old One's shed scale.
Then the Choir came singing up the pass and took it. I'm the last founder. I'm not leaving.
I'm not leaving, keeper. Someone has to remember how it's done.
You've been inside. Then you've felt it. They've stoked it white-hot.
They're melting the Ember Bell down into something that wakes. Pull it out, keeper.
You pulled the Ember Bell out of my crucible. Not one founder before me managed that.
My forge is lit again, thanks to you. Here. Brinesteel, poured from bell-metal.
It'll ring when it strikes true. Mind you listen for it.
The forge stays lit now. Come back if that blade ever dulls.
Put your backs into it. The bell's under her, and Vael wants it before the tide turns.
A keeper's child, all the way down here? Go home, little lamp. This is bigger than you.
She's waking! Leave the bar. Down the holes, both of you. Now!
Work those bellows! It has to run like water before the tide turns.
You again, little lamp? Too late. We'll pour it into a Waking Bell.
The slag's alive! Get back from the rim. Out, all of you!
Little lamp. You hauled me out of the Belfry. Don't expect thanks.
The others folded their robes and went home. Where's home, for me?
Half my life I followed Vael. Now he's down there, singing it to sleep.
I'll stand watch out here. Somebody has to, and it won't be you.
Oh... look at them. Every light in the fen, dreaming the same shape.
That's a calf. The Old One isn't angry. It's grieving, and they're its dreams.
I sang them out of their lanterns for Vael. I won't do it again. Not for anyone.
Keeper. Wick lets me help with the lights now. I owe the fen that.
I sang the lights out of them once. Now I hum them home.
It's slower. The lights don't mind. Neither do I.
Wick counts the lanterns. I count with them. I keep losing count.
It turned over in its sleep. I felt it in my teeth, like a low hymn.
The strange lights went out to sea last night. They were singing.
The Marrow Tomb: Hall of Ribs
The Marrow Tomb: the Regent's Barrow
The Echo Horn! A curl of old bone bound in gold. Blow it, and the barrow answers.
Press its item key (U or I) to blow one long note. Bone that hears it shatters, and things that hide are shown.
Wren rings the Marrow Bell. Its soft note goes out over the dunes, over every bone in the sand.
The Old One's kin sleep there too. Far under the bay, it breathes out, slow as an ebbing tide.
So you carry Hessa's lamp now. I carried it once, before you were born.
I was her first apprentice. She taught me the lullaby, just as she's teaching you.
But I listened too closely. Under every phrase, the Old One is weeping.
Ring the bell, and listen. Then tell me we should keep singing it to sleep.
Many voices sing from the bay
A deep rumble from under the sea
You've met him, then. Vael. I felt the whole coast turn over in its sleep.
He was my apprentice. Best ear I ever trained. He said the Old One was weeping.
I couldn't hear it. My ears were already going. So I told him he was wrong.
And then I stopped listening to him at all. That's on me, not him.
Don't hate him, child. He's wrong, but he isn't cruel.
Ottilie trained alongside us, once. She fishes Still Cove now. Go and see her.
Seven bells, and Hessa's lamp. You came all this way to sing it back under.
Listen to it, keeper. Then let the Choir finish its song.
...Wait. Your notes. All seven, in order. I never heard them like that.
It isn't weeping. It's dreaming badly, and nobody has sat with it.
I was right that it suffers. I was wrong about the cure. Go on. Its heart is waking.
Wren hums the last line: "Sleep, old heart, sleep."
Deep below, the Old One hums back. For the first time, it sleeps in peace.
So the Regent's gone to bones at last. Then you've earned this. Come, look.
Those bones out on the dunes were its family. It lay down beside them to grieve.
The Regent wanted a weapon. All it ever wanted was to sleep where they sleep.
Whatever that Choir hears weeping, child, it isn't anger. Go and ring your bell.
Back with the bones, child? They're quieter now. So is it.
It dreams of them, I think. Not grieving now. Remembering.
Sit a while, if you like. The dead don't mind company.
The Nacre Buckler! Mother-of-pearl, grown over a bell-ringer's shield in the dark.
The Abyssal Coat! Cut from something that lived far deeper than this. It is heavier than it looks.
The Tidecaller! A keeper's blade, lost in the Old One's mouth long ago. It hums with the tide.
It's asleep. Really asleep. I've never once heard it this quiet.
I'll stay. Someone should sit with it while it dreams. I'll know if it stirs.
Tell Hessa I'm listening now. She'll know what that means. Go home, keeper.
At dawn, Mantle came gliding down to the mouth of the Maw.
Wren rode home over a calm sea, with the sun coming up behind them.
Hessa knelt on the warm boards, laid her palm flat on them, and waited.
Far off under the bay, the Point Bell rang. She felt every note of it.
The boats went out on a gentle tide. The grey robes were folded away.
And far below, the Old One slept, and dreamed of nothing at all.
Wait! Please. You're the lamp keeper's kid? I'm Tobin. I sang with the Choir.
They've all gone down into the Maw, off Lullaby Point. They'll sing the Waking Song till dawn.
You go in under the Old One's lip, where the rock's warm. Its breath'll knock you flat.
Vael says it'll wake gentle. It won't. I heard it, down in the Tomb.
I'm going home. If my dad will have me.
Dad. I'm sorry. They said the song would make the sea quiet again. It was a lie.
Your bed's still made. I made it up fresh every week. Every week, Tobin.
Get that robe off. There's a jumper of yours in the chest. Then come and help me with the rope.
Keeper. He says you stopped and listened to him. Hm. Thank you.
Boy ties a knot like a gull. He'll learn. Hm.
Dad hasn't stopped talking since I got back. I didn't know he had this many words.
The sea's breathing slow again. I can hear it from the dock. Thank you, keeper.
Seven bells, all rung. I felt every one of them come up through the floorboards.
The tide's out tonight. Fetch the oars. I'll row you to the Maw myself.
There you are. I felt the last bell ring, and I took the boat out to find you.
There's its lip, and the door the singers use. Vael's in there, with all of them.
He was a good boy once. He heard what I couldn't. Bring him out, if he'll come.
I'll keep the lamp lit at home. Look for it when you come up.
Ide. I ferry folk over the channel when the water lets me. It hasn't let me in weeks.
Something's ringing wrong under the water south of here. Till it stops, my boat stays tied.
That bell's gone quiet. The channel's sitting still for the first time in weeks.
In you get, keeper. Sit low, and mind the oar.
The whole sea's lying still. I'd row you anywhere today. Over we go.
Liesl. That cottage on the flats was my family's, gran after gran, way back.
I keep the lane swept, so it's tidy when the water goes out.
The night the Verge Bell went quiet, the sea came up this lane.
It never went home again. They say she was laying the table.
Her little door bell hung by that step for three hundred years.
The tide tore it off last winter. It'll be out on the square's flats.
If you're on the square's flats at low tide, look for a glint in the sand. Brass, about so big.
That's it. That's her bell. Look, you can still see where she polished it.
I'll hang it back by her door. Here, take these.
Old Verge coins turn up in the sand. She'd want you to have them.
Wren found a little brass door bell in the sand.
Every low tide now her bell rings out there on its own, so she knows someone's still home.
Did you hear it? The Verge Bell's ringing again.
And her little one rings back. Three hundred years she waited.
The sea's gone soft. Some mornings I think the tide's swept the step for me.
I'm Wick. Every night I count the lanterns.
One for every family's dead, so they can find their way home.
Five of them have gone dark, out in the fen.
And there are more lights than lanterns now. Lights that aren't anyone's.
My pole can't reach past the deep water. If you've a light of your own, could you light them again?
Still dark ones. Glowcap Grove, Witherroot, Glowworm Hollow, Stillwater, Lumen Pool. I count every night.
All of them! I counted twice. Everyone can find their way home tonight.
Here. Gran kept lamp oil in this. It's empty, but it's a good jar.
Every lantern lit, and the extra lights keep their distance now. I think they were only lonely.
The fen's other lights went out to sea last night, one by one.
Not ours. The other ones. I counted them leaving.
Hm? Oh. Not asleep. Resting my eyes. Gully, salvager.
This old girl? Figurehead off the Lantern Wake. The keepers' own ship.
The keepers rang bells off her deck, back when there were bells.
Then a storm took her down, crew and all. Long before my time.
The tide turned on me last week. Took my strongbox into the pool.
Too deep to wade. Got anything with reach to it?
Still bobbing out there. Hook it and haul, keeper.
That's her! Barnacled shut, but that's mine. Good haul.
Here. A salvager's cut. Fair's fair.
Wren hauled a barnacled strongbox out of the pool.
I keep her company. She kept the keepers'.
Longer on this strand than anyone remembers. She's earned a rest.
Felt the whole strand shift last night. She felt it too.
Sea's gone calm. Even she looks like she's sleeping now.
Captain Sorrel, Gullwatch kite-post. Retired. Don't salute.
Forty years I flew the post across this water by kite.
Letters for the Spire, medicine for the mills. Never lost one.
Then the bells went quiet, the gales turned mean, and we shut.
If you ever learn to catch the wind, come and race my kite.
No wings on you yet. The Spire's where the wind's kept.
That's a kite cloak on your back! The keepers' old pattern.
Race my kite to the post on the far bank. First there wins.
The water's narrow here. The wind's yours if you're brave.
Again? Good. She's itching to fly.
Don't stand there talking, she's flying! Go!
Beat my kite fair and square! Not seen that in forty years.
Here. A courier's pay for a courier's run.
Your pennant's flying on the far post. Gullwatch remembers.
Maybe I'll open the post again, once the gales calm down.
The winds are gentle now. I've started flying letters again.
Hessa's keeper, are you? She always did send me the quiet ones.
Shh. You'll spook the rimefin. Ottilie. I fish this cove.
Rimefin only bite when the cove's still, and it hasn't been.
Something big down there turns in its sleep. Fish scatter.
My old fingers are too slow for them now. Yours look quick.
Sit by the hole there. Float goes under, you pull. Three'll do me.
Still waiting on my three. Eyes on the float, now.
Three! Look at the frost on their fins. Supper for a week.
Take these. Old keepers' coin, from when I trained up here.
The cove's still today. Even the deep sleeps easier.
Hessa, Vael and I trained in the old cave above. Cold years.
Vael would lie with his ear to the ice for hours. Listening.
He heard it first, you know. The Old One, grieving.
The ice sings at night now. Soft, like someone humming.
Mind where you step, I've glass drying on the sand. I'm Coralie.
Sea-glass. Old bottles the tide's tumbled smooth for years.
Hang it on a string and the wind makes it ring. Listen.
My chime's bare, though. The sea hides its glass well.
Twelve strings, and hardly a piece on them. Bring me what you find? I'll pay.
Twelve strings to fill. Glass hides in quiet corners.
Oh, lovely. Hear that? Every piece rings a little different.
Wren got 25 Glints for each piece.
That's twelve! Every string has its glass. Hush a moment.
Hear that? The whole shore's ringing with it.
Take the rest of my savings, too. Chimes don't need coin.
Every wind plays a different tune now. Today's is a slow one.
The chime rang all by itself last night. Low, like a sigh.
The wind and the tide keep time together now. Hear them?
Felt the whole bay shift last night. Every boat dragged its anchor.
Nets are full again, keeper. Sea's breathing like it should.
Did you feel the ground roll over? Mum says I dreamed it. I didn't.
Me and Mum listened to the sea all night. It snores!
The sea moved! I flashed 'I'm here' at it. Just in case.
Can I carry your lamp? Just to the end of the dock? Please?
Felt the Old One turn from up here. Every coal in the Kiln rang.
Every bell rings true now. Founders' work, and yours.
The racks shook in the night and the eels all fled. Is it waking?
Supper's on, keeper. Eel. Don't argue. Sit.
Hm. Ground moved. Gulls went quiet. ...Tobin's out there somewhere.
Hm. Quiet now. The good kind.
The fen shook in the night. Every lantern held. I counted.
The Storm Bell's rung and the gales have eased. I feel it in the cloth.
Keeper. When we shut the post, three letters never went out.
They've sat in my satchel ever since, nagging at me.
One for Ottilie at the cove, one for Liesl on the Verge, one for Agna at the Kiln.
See them home and there's courier's pay in it. Fly safe.
Wren tucks the three letters away.
Still got my letters? Ottilie, Liesl, Agna. They've waited long enough.
All three delivered! Far as I'm concerned, the post's open again.
Here's your pay. You'd make a fine courier, keeper.
Wren hands over a letter from Sorrel's satchel.
A letter? From my sister, at the mills. I'd know her hand anywhere.
A grandson! Two months old already. I'll knit him a hat.
For me? It's from the Spire. Someone asking after Gran's cottage.
A painter wants to paint it at low tide. Well. She'd have liked that.
An order? The Spire wants a new bell for its weathervane.
Founders' work, at last. Tell Sorrel I'll send my answer by kite.
Hessa's told you, then. About Vael, and the cave.
We quarrelled when he left. I stopped visiting. So did she.
Show her this with your lamp: three quick flashes, then a long glow.
Our cave sign. 'Still here, still friends.' She'll know it.
Three quick, then long. Show Hessa, before I lose my nerve.
Wren flashes the lamp three times, quick, then holds a long glow.
Three and a long... Ottilie's sign. I'd know it in my sleep.
Tell her yes. The kettle's been on since the day she stopped coming.
Once... that's yes. She'll have the kettle on. Always far too strong.
I'll walk down to Saltmarrow when the ice lets me. Here, for the road.
Murmur helps me count now. Murmur's good at it. Mostly.
But there's no lantern out there for Murmur's family.
Murmur won't say the family name. Only that they were singers, from the Verge.
Liesl on the Verge knows everyone's gran. Can you ask her?
Have you asked Liesl yet? If anyone remembers Murmur's people, she will.
Singers from the Verge? That'll be the Reeds. Lovely voices, all of them.
Their door was three down from Gran's. Tell Wick: the Reeds.
The Reeds! I've made the lantern already. It only wants lighting.
Wren lights the new lantern from the Glowmoth Lantern's flame.
Don't tell Murmur. Let Murmur find it. I'll watch from here.
There's a new lantern down by the water. Someone's tied a tag to it. It says Reed.
I haven't said that name since I put on the grey.
...Thank you, keeper. And Wick. I'll keep it lit.
The Reed lantern burns steady. My family would have liked it here.
Words are cut into the stone, worn almost smooth.
Row upon row of small notches are cut into the stone, from top to bottom.
One for every tide rung on time. Near the ground, someone has started a new row.
Here the keepers' round begins. Ring at every turning, keeper, and come home.
H., keeper of the Point. Rang all seven alone again this year. Will again next year.
The wood creeps over the path a little more each spring. Cut it back. Keep the way.
Seven bells from the Kiln's fire and the scale the Old One shed. Founders' work.
Holt, bell-founder, walked this far to hear the Ember Bell ring. It rang true.
Hang a lantern for any keeper who sleeps in the fen. Wick it, and they'll find home.
Here Morrow first heard it humming, they say. Hush, keeper, and listen.
The wind wears the words away up here. Cut them deeper.
V., apprentice. Rang the Storm Bell in a real storm. H. says I'm showing off.
H., V. and O. were here. Three apprentices, one cave, and no feeling in our toes.
O. was here first. O. is always here first.
The Verge Bell went quiet for one season. The Verge went under in one night.
For the Verge, under the flats. We missed one season once. Never again.
Old bones. Walk softly, keeper, and keep your voice low.
The dunes belong to the bone-readers. Ask before you walk them, keeper.
The Lantern Wake: keepers met here to eat and sing. Bring bread. Bring a friend.
Pour slow. Cool slower. A bell cast in a hurry rings false.
The wisps are only dreams. Don't follow them. Do sing to them.
The top bell turns the verse. Ring it gently. It is heavier than it looks.
H. and V., apprentices. Perfect pitch, both. (V. more so.) (He is not.)

Wick's lights in Gloamfen keep going out. I can see the fen gone dark from the gallery.
Rocks came down past Wreck Strand. That mallet you brought out of the Kiln will shift them.
The Storm Bell's at the top of the Spire, child. Up on Windmere Heights, where the wind lives.
Go north through the wood to Gullwatch. The old keepers' planks there only show for a lantern.

Go when the tide's out, child. Or turn it yourself, at a stone.
One bell left. Dace's people keep the Ossuary Dunes, out past Tangle Shore.
Deep water lies between. You'll want something to breathe with under it.
The Maw's waiting, child. Go on. The lamp stays lit.
Dry ground on the Ebb Shelf! Never thought I'd stand out here without a boat.
See her? A lantern-boat. Ran aground here in the big storm, twelve years back.
Empty, folk said. But Hessa rowed out that night, and came home with her coat buttoned up.
Twelve years, near enough... Go on, keeper. Have a look.
I'll not take a thing from that boat. Whatever's in her is yours.
Found something, did you? Keep it close. The sea doesn't give much back.
A little lantern-boat, half buried in the sand. Its lamp hook still hangs at the bow.
Under the bench, wedged in the boards: a child's knitted cap, stiff with salt.
Wren turns it over and over. It would fit a very small head.
Only sand now. The lamp hook creaks when the wind finds it.
Wren holds out the little cap from the lantern-boat.
Where did you... Out on the Shelf. Of course. You held the tide out.
Hessa holds the cap a long time. Then she folds it, and puts it back in Wren's hands.
Keep it, child. Keep it close.
East of the Spire there's a run of sea stacks the gulls own. Gullcry, we called it.
No courier ever flew it end to end. I never dared. You might.
You flew Gullcry? End to end? The gulls will be talking about it for a week.
Half my life I wanted to see that done. Thank you, keeper.
South of Mirelight there's a hollow with four old braziers. Nobody's lit them in my life.
Gran called it the Lampless Sink. I can't count what I can't see.
The Sink's lit! I saw the glow from here. Four. I counted.
Now I've four more to count every night. Thank you.
Past Vertebra Road lies a ring of old ribs. Our young went there to prove their nerve.
Stand in it, and the dunes send what they send. Then come back and sit with me.
You stood the Ring? Then the dunes know your face now, child.
Few keepers ever tried it. Fewer came back smiling.
Every keeper cuts a line into the Tidestones. Vael and I walked the round once, reading them all.
Twenty-two of them, shore to dunes. Read every one, child, then come and tell me.
You've read every stone. I can see it on you. Every keeper back to Morrow.
Then there's one line missing. Fetch my old knife from the drawer.
Hessa walks out to the Tidestone at Wreck Hollow, and cuts into it for a long while.
There. Under mine. Go and read it, keeper.
And W., keeper of the Point. Rang all seven. Not alone.

Bram, Sela, Pim and Ansel. Ashamed, I think. Or afraid of what's waiting.
Last I heard: one in Cinderreach, one up the Frostspine, one in the fen, one on the Heights.
Find them, keeper. Not for me. For whoever's still leaving a light on.
Bram, Sela, Pim and Ansel. I count them the way a keeper counts bells.
All four home. The gulls told me, and a kite came by with a note.
Then I've no Choir left to keep.
Sister Lowe slips off her grey robe, folds it, and sets it down on the rocks.
Just Lowe, now. Take this. I won't be needing the Choir's purse.
Just Lowe. It'll take some getting used to. The sea doesn't seem to mind.
Go away. ...Sorry. I'm Bram. I sang with the Choir.

Agna won't want me back. I wouldn't want me.
Bram? That great lump. Too much coal, every time. I'd know his stoking anywhere.
Tell him the forge needs a bellows-hand. He can come and get burnt like the rest of us.
Wren mimes working a bellows, then points the way to the Kiln.
Then I'd best not keep her waiting. Thank you, keeper.
Too much coal, she says. Every time. I'm learning.
Don't tell anyone you found me. I'm Sela. I'm only resting.

I'll go home soon. Tomorrow. Or the day after.
Sela? My sister's girl, out in the cold in a grey sheet? Oh, that child.

Wren points back toward Still Cove, then mimes rocking a baby.
Aunt Ottilie? She'd walk me home?

Is the singing over? I'm Pim. I was the littlest one in the Choir.

It's so dark past the trees. I'll wait for a light.
Wren raises the Glowmoth Lantern high.
Oh! It's like the lanterns at home.

Ah. A keeper. Ansel, once of the Gullwatch post. Lately of the Choir, the old fool.

My knees won't carry me home over the chasm. And who wants an old singer back?
I'll just sit with the sea a while longer.
Ansel? My old sorter? He's alive? The old goose!
Tell him the post's open and the letters are piling up. I'll fly a kite to fetch him.
Wren points up. A red kite is coming in over the cliffs.
That's Sorrel's kite! She's sent for me?
Then I'm going home by air, keeper. At my age. Imagine.
Tell her I'm walking down to the mills to see my sister. She can walk with me.
Aunt Ottilie walks fast. I'd better catch her up.
I'm going, I'm going! Keep the light up.
Wave to Sorrel for me, keeper. I'll be the one in the sky.
Ha! A lamp, this far out. I thought I was the only fool up here.
Ferrin. I map the edges, where the world stops bothering.
My knees won't take the far reaches now. Yours might.
One past the Frostspine, one past Cinderreach, one off the bottom of the Verge.
Drive each in where the land gives out. I'll know. I always know.
Ferrin hands Wren three striped survey stakes.
Stakes still in your bag? The edges won't come to us, keeper.
Wren drives a striped stake in, right where the land gives out.
Ferrin's stake stands firm, its little flag snapping in the wind.
All three in! I felt every one, like a tooth coming through.
Ferrin unrolls his map and inks in the last lines, slow and careful.
There. All of it. Smaller than I thought. And bigger.
For your trouble. Mapmakers are poor, but not that poor.
Hessa keeps her lamp. I keep the edges. Everyone keeps something.
Three stones, piled with care. Someone meant to mark this spot.
A whale's skull, no bigger than a rowboat, sunk to the jaw in the fen.
Fen-lights rest on the bone, the way moths settle on a warm lamp.
Wren hums, very low. Far below, for a moment, something hums back.
The fen-lights rest on the little skull. They don't mind Wren.
A grey Choir robe lies folded on the little skull. Fen-lights sleep on it.

You found the little one. Out past the last of the lanterns.

Now it keeps the little one warm. That's what it's for, I think.
Lines are scratched into the rock, one above another, each a hand higher.

The name by that line is Liesl, and next to it, a tiny bell.

A Liesl on the grotto wall, with a little bell beside her?

She didn't. She climbed, and counted, and waited.
She lived. That's why there's a me. I'll set her a place tonight.
